summary.text: The Pauli exclusion principle says that two or more identical particles with half-integer spin, called fermions, cannot occupy the same quantum state at once.
Wolfgang Pauli formulated it in 1925 for electrons, which is why two electrons in one orbital must have opposite spins.
It underpins the large-scale stability of matter and the chemical behavior of atoms, while bosons such as photons are free to share states.

facts.label: Formulated
facts.value: By Wolfgang Pauli in 1925, for electrons

facts.label: Extended in
facts.value: 1940, to all fermions via the spin–statistics theorem

facts.label: Who obeys it
facts.value: Quarks, electrons, neutrinos, protons and neutrons

facts.label: Who is exempt
facts.value: Bosons, such as photons and Cooper pairs

facts.label: Why it works
facts.value: Fermion wave functions flip sign when two are swapped

items.prompt: Two electrons sit in the same orbital with identical n, ℓ and m_ℓ. What must be true of their spins?

options.label: They must be opposite
They must be identical
They must both be zero
Spin plays no role

items.explain: Two electrons cannot share all four quantum numbers, so with the other three equal, one must have spin +1/2 and the other −1/2.

items.prompt: A laser beam packs enormous numbers of photons into the same state. Why doesn't exclusion forbid it?

options.label: Lasers break the law of physics
Photons are too small to count
Lasers are not made of light
Photons are bosons, which may share a state

items.explain: Particles with integer spin are not subject to the exclusion principle, and any number of identical bosons can share a state, such as photons in a laser.

items.prompt: Helium-3 and helium-4 atoms differ in total spin. What follows?

options.label: Both are fermions
Helium-3 is a fermion and helium-4 a boson
Both are bosons
Helium-3 is a boson and helium-4 a fermion

items.explain: Helium-3 has spin 1/2 and is a fermion, whereas helium-4 has spin 0 and is a boson.

items.prompt: Why can two identical fermions not occupy one state, in terms of the wave function?

options.label: The wave function would need to grow
They would repel with infinite force
Their electric charges would cancel out
A swap must flip the sign yet change nothing

items.explain: For fermions swapping two particles flips the sign of the wave function, but identical states would leave it unchanged; only a function that is zero everywhere does both, so such a state cannot exist.

items.prompt: Before Pauli, chemists noted that shells seemed to fill with certain numbers of electrons such as 2, 8 and 18. What did Pauli do?

options.label: Showed the numbers were just random
Found a one-electron-per-state rule
Denied that shells existed at all
Traced the numbers to the nucleus

items.explain: He reduced the complicated closed-shell numbers to one electron per state by adding a two-valued quantum number, identified as electron spin.

items.prompt: Which particles are fermions and so obey the exclusion principle?

options.label: Photons and W bosons
Cooper pairs and photons
Protons and neutrons
Z bosons and photons

items.explain: Baryons such as protons and neutrons are fermions, as are quarks, electrons and neutrinos, while photons and W and Z bosons are bosons.

paragraphs.heading: One state, one fermion
paragraphs.text: The Pauli exclusion principle says that two or more identical particles with half-integer spin cannot be in the same quantum state at the same time. Such particles are called fermions. Half-integer spin means their built-in angular momentum is the reduced Planck constant ℏ times 1/2, 3/2, 5/2 and so on. Wolfgang Pauli stated the rule for electrons in 1925, and in 1940 his spin–statistics theorem extended it to all fermions.

paragraphs.heading: Electrons in an atom
paragraphs.text: For electrons in an atom, the rule says no two of them can share the same values of all four quantum numbers: n, ℓ, m_ℓ and the spin quantum number mₛ. Two electrons in one orbital already share n, ℓ and m_ℓ, so their spins must differ. Spin can only be +1/2 or −1/2, so one electron takes each value.

paragraphs.heading: Who must obey it
paragraphs.text: Fermions include quarks, electrons and neutrinos, along with protons and neutrons, which are each made of three quarks. Whole atoms can be fermions too, depending on their overall spin: helium-3 has spin 1/2 and is a fermion, while helium-4 has spin 0 and is a boson. Bosons are particles with whole-number spin, and the rule does not bind them. Any number of identical bosons can share one state, as photons from a laser or atoms in a Bose–Einstein condensate do.

paragraphs.heading: Why it holds
paragraphs.text: The deeper reason lies in what happens when two identical particles swap places. For fermions the total wave function flips sign, while for bosons it stays the same. Now picture two fermions in exactly the same state: swapping them changes nothing, yet the sign must still flip. The only function that can do both is one that is zero everywhere, so that state cannot exist.

paragraphs.heading: Shells and the periodic table
paragraphs.text: In the early 1900s it became clear that atoms and molecules with even numbers of electrons were more chemically stable. In 1919 Irving Langmuir suggested the periodic table could be explained if electrons were clustered in some way, and groups of them were thought to sit in shells around the nucleus. In 1922 Bohr took certain numbers of electrons, such as 2, 8 and 18, to form stable closed shells. Pauli set out to explain these numbers, which at first came only from experiment. A 1924 paper by Stoner gave him a clue, and he saw that the shell numbers reduce to one electron per state if each state is labeled with four quantum numbers.

paragraphs.heading: Spin and everyday matter
paragraphs.text: For this, Pauli brought in a new quantum number with just two values, and Samuel Goudsmit and George Uhlenbeck identified it as electron spin. The exclusion principle underpins many properties of ordinary matter, from its stability on a large scale to the chemical behavior of atoms. Bosons, particles with whole-number spin that escape the rule, include the photon, the Cooper pairs responsible for superconductivity, and the W and Z bosons.
